title: Why can't anyone forecast this bar?
hook: A bar is fun with 60 people and awful with more. Everyone trusts one good forecast. Then?

knows: network effects make things more valuable as more people join
doesNotKnow: that with a crowding cost, any forecast everyone believes makes itself wrong

misconception: If everyone uses the same good forecast, the bar will be pleasantly busy.
objective: The learner can explain why a shared forecast of a crowded resource defeats itself (low sends everyone, high sends no one), and why even randomising leaves the bar crowded on nearly half the nights.

claims.text: If all 100 people act on the same forecast, all 100 come when it says 60 or fewer and nobody comes when it says more.
claims.source: The lesson's rule (each goes only if they expect 60 or fewer) applied to one shared forecast; Demo.tsx attendanceFor(): 50 → 100, 70 → 0. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): attendanceFor(): f <= 60 -> 100, else 0; reveal prints attendanceFor(50) = 100 and attendanceFor(70) = 0.

claims.text: Any forecast everyone believes makes itself wrong.
claims.source: From c1: a believed forecast of 60 or fewer produces 100; a believed forecast above 60 produces 0; neither outcome matches the forecast. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): within the lesson's model every believed forecast f gives 100 (f <= 60) or 0 (f > 60), so outcome = forecast would need f = 100 with f <= 60 or f = 0 with f > 60: impossible.

claims.text: If each person goes independently with probability 0.6, on average 60 come, and attendance is above 60 on 46.2% of nights in the long run.
claims.source: Binomial(100, 0.6): mean 60; P(X > 60) = sum over k = 61..100 = 0.4621. Re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02); matches the brief. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): own log-space binomial sum (scratchpad fc22/bar.mjs): P(X > 60) = 0.46208 for Binomial(100, 0.6); mean 60. | v2: reveal adds 'so on average 60 come' (100 × 0.6 = 60). | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own log-space binomial sum (fc24/bar.mjs): P(X > 60) = 0.46208 for Binomial(100, 0.6); mean 100 × 0.6 = 60. v2 reveal wording '(so on average 60 come)' and '46.2%' match; paragraph renders only once a run is recorded (best), which milestone mixed-100 guarantees.

claims.text: The learner's longest random run (recorded when it is run, kept after Reset; 111 nights on the QA path) shows an average near 60 with a crowded share near half.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: mulberry32(1), 100 draws per night, each goes if r() < 0.6. Seed 1 was the first seed tried, not chosen for the result. Seed 1: 100 nights average 60.2, 48 crowded; 200 nights 60.3, 96 crowded. Seeds 2 and 3 at 100 nights: 38 and 44 crowded. The reveal quotes the learner's run. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): own mulberry32 re-implementation: seed 1 at 100 nights avg 60.2, 48 crowded; 111 nights (QA path) 60.1, 54; 200 nights 60.3, 96; every run length from 100 to 500 gives crowded share 44.4-51.6% and average 59.9-60.5. Seeds 2 and 3: 38 and 44 crowded at 100. Non-blocking note: Reset after the milestone lets the reveal quote a run under 100 nights (e.g. 1 night: 100% crowded); the numbers quoted are still the learner's own. | v2: v2 records the longest run (nights, average, crowded %) and the reveal quotes the record, so Reset cannot turn it into '0 nights'. With seed 1: 111 nights average 60.1, 49% crowded (builder node re-run of mulberry32(1), 2026-10-14). | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own mulberry32(1) replay, 100 draws per night: 111 nights avg 60.1, 49% crowded (Math.round); 100 nights 60.2, 48%; every recordable longest run (100..500 nights, since mixed-100 needs >= 100 and best only grows) gives avg 59.9-60.5 and 44-52% crowded, so 'near 60' and 'near half' hold on every path. Reset clears chart and readouts but not best/fc, and re-running restarts the same stream, so the record cannot shrink.

claims.text: The average sits right at the limit, so nearly half the nights land above it.
This is a model of Arthur's El Farol bar problem (1994): identical people, one shared forecast, no learning.
claims.source: W. B. Arthur, 'Inductive reasoning and bounded rationality', American Economic Review 84(2), 406-411 (1994; title and pages from memory). Model simplifications are the lesson's. The book chapter placement (Easley and Kleinberg 2010 ch. 17) is not cited to learners until the fact-checker confirms it. Fact-checker confirms attribution. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Arthur, 'Inductive Reasoning and Bounded Rationality', AER 84(2) Papers and Proceedings, 406-411 (May 1994): confirmed bibliographically via search (JSTOR/IDEAS listings); full text host blocked, not opened. The 100-person, 60-seat setup is the well-known El Farol framing (from knowledge, consistent with secondary sources in search). 'Identical people, one shared forecast, no learning' is presented as the lesson's simplification, which is accurate. E&K placement: ch. 17 is 'Network Effects' (library catalogue TOC via search); El Farol as its closing advanced section on negative externalities is from memory (fairly sure, section number 17.7 not confirmed). Not shown to learners.

recall.question: A free museum is pleasant with up to 300 visitors. An app tells everyone '200 visitors expected today', and everyone believes it. What happens?
options: Far more than 300 come, because everyone expects room
recall.why: A believed low forecast sends everyone, which makes the forecast wrong. When more is worse, no forecast everyone trusts can be right.
